title: Separation of Powers
body: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that legislative, executive and judicial power should be held by different bodies. The idea strongly shaped the United States Constitution and modern democracies.

title: Women's Suffrage
body: In 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections. Most Western countries followed in the first half of the 20th century, often after long campaigns by the suffrage movement.

title: The United Nations
body: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and the organisation formally came into being that autumn. The five permanent members of the Security Council hold a veto: the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France.

title: The Freedom of the Press Act of 1766
body: Sweden's 1766 act is regarded as the world's first constitutional protection of press freedom. It also introduced an early form of the principle of public access to official documents.

title: The European Union
body: The Treaty of Rome of 1957 created the European Economic Community. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 founded the European Union and laid the ground for the single currency.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
body: The UN General Assembly adopted the declaration on 10 December 1948. The drafting commission was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It is not binding in itself but has inspired a series of binding human rights treaties.

title: Athenian Democracy
body: Reforms by Cleisthenes around 508 BC gave Athens a system in which citizens voted directly on laws in the assembly. Only adult male citizens took part, excluding women, slaves and foreigners, but it is the best-known early democracy.

title: The United States Constitution
body: Drafted in Philadelphia in 1787, it is one of the oldest written national constitutions still in force. It divides power between three branches and between federal and state governments. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, were added in 1791.

title: NATO
body: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization was founded in 1949 as a Western defence alliance. Its core is Article 5: an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

title: The Rule of Law
body: The rule of law means that everyone, including those in power, is subject to laws that are public, clear and applied equally by independent courts. It is distinct from 'rule by law', where law is merely a tool of those in power.

title: The Westminster System
body: Named after the British Parliament, this system makes the government depend on the confidence of an elected parliament. The prime minister and cabinet sit in parliament and can be removed by it. It has been adopted in many former British colonies.

title: The Geneva Conventions
body: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 protected wounded soldiers. The four conventions of 1949 extend protection to the sick, shipwrecked, prisoners of war and civilians, and form the core of international humanitarian law.

title: Duverger's Law
body: Political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post voting tends to produce two dominant parties, while proportional representation favours many parties. It is a tendency rather than a strict law, but it helps explain differences between party systems.

title: The Beveridge Report
body: William Beveridge's 1942 report proposed a comprehensive system of social insurance in Britain to fight 'want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness'. It laid the ground for the post-war British welfare state, including the National Health Service.

title: What Makes a State
body: The Montevideo Convention of 1933 sets out four widely cited criteria for statehood: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Recognition by other states is a separate question.

title: The European Convention on Human Rights
body: Signed in Rome in 1950 by members of the Council of Europe, the convention protects civil and political rights such as the right to life, a fair trial and freedom of expression. Its distinctive feature is the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, to which individuals can bring cases against states. It is separate from the European Union.

title: The Gadaa System
body: Gadaa is the traditional system of self-government of the Oromo people of Ethiopia and Kenya, organising men into generation grades that pass through successive stages of eight years each. Leaders are elected for a single eight-year term and power passes peacefully from one group to the next. UNESCO inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage in 2016.

title: Pancasila
body: Proclaimed by Sukarno in 1945, Pancasila ('five principles') is the founding philosophy of the Indonesian state: belief in one God, a just and civilised humanity, the unity of Indonesia, democracy guided by deliberation, and social justice. Its broad monotheism was designed to unite a religiously diverse nation without making it an Islamic state.

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
body: In this 1792 book Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women seem inferior only because they are denied a proper education, and that they should be educated as rational beings and equal companions to men. Written in response to the revolutionary debates on rights in France and Britain, it is regarded as a founding text of liberal feminism.

title: Brazil's Golden Law
body: Signed by Princess Isabel on 13 May 1888, the Lei Áurea abolished slavery in Brazil without compensation to slave owners. Brazil had received more enslaved Africans than any other country in the Americas and was the last nation in the Western Hemisphere to end slavery. The monarchy fell the following year, partly because it had lost the support of landowners.

title: Justinian's Code
body: In the 520s and 530s the Byzantine emperor Justinian I had centuries of Roman law collected and systematised in what later became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis. Rediscovered in Western Europe around 1100 and studied at Bologna, it became the basis of the civil law tradition used across continental Europe, Latin America and beyond.

title: The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
body: From 1977 mothers whose children had been 'disappeared' by Argentina's military dictatorship marched each week in front of the presidential palace in Buenos Aires, wearing white headscarves. Their protest defied a regime that banned public gatherings and drew world attention to state terror. Related groups later worked to trace children taken from detained parents.

title: The English Bill of Rights
body: Passed in 1689 after the Glorious Revolution placed William III and Mary II on the throne, the Bill of Rights barred the Crown from suspending laws, levying taxes or keeping a standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. It also protected free elections and freedom of speech in Parliament. It is a cornerstone of constitutional monarchy and influenced the American Bill of Rights.

title: Nepal's Abolition of the Monarchy
body: After a decade-long Maoist insurgency and mass protests in 2006, Nepal's newly elected Constituent Assembly abolished the centuries-old Shah monarchy in May 2008 and declared a federal democratic republic. After years of deadlock, a new constitution was adopted in 2015.

title: From the OAU to the African Union
body: The Organisation of African Unity was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963 to support decolonisation and defend the sovereignty of new states, but its principle of non-interference kept it largely silent on abuses within them. It was replaced in 2002 by the African Union, whose founding act allows intervention in a member state in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

title: The Mandate of Heaven
body: The Zhou dynasty, which overthrew the Shang in the 11th century BC, justified its rule by claiming that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a corrupt one. Natural disasters and revolts could be read as signs that the mandate had been lost. The idea legitimised both imperial rule and successful rebellion throughout Chinese history.

title: UN Peacekeeping
body: The first UN military observer mission was sent to the Middle East in 1948, and the first armed peacekeeping force was deployed in 1956 during the Suez Crisis. Blue-helmeted peacekeepers, contributed by member states and lightly armed, monitor ceasefires and help carry out peace agreements, normally with the consent of the parties. UN peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.

title: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
body: In the Muqaddimah (1377), the North African scholar Ibn Khaldun argued that dynasties rise on asabiyyah, the group solidarity of hardy, often nomadic peoples, and decline as luxury erodes it, typically within a few generations. His cyclical theory of how states form and fall has earned him a place among the forerunners of sociology and political science.

title: The American Civil Rights Movement
body: Through boycotts, sit-ins and marches, including the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–56 sparked by Rosa Parks and the 1963 March on Washington, African Americans challenged segregation and disenfranchisement in the South. Led by figures such as Martin Luther King Jr., the movement won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

title: The Cyrus Cylinder
body: This clay cylinder, inscribed in Akkadian after Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, describes how he restored temples and allowed displaced peoples to return home. It is sometimes called the first charter of human rights, but most historians regard that label as anachronistic, since the text follows a traditional Mesopotamian genre of royal propaganda.

title: The May Fourth Movement
body: On 4 May 1919 students in Beijing protested against the Paris Peace Conference's decision to transfer Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan rather than return them to China. The protests grew into a broad cultural and political movement championing science, democracy and writing in vernacular Chinese. Its activists included several founders of the Chinese Communist Party, established in 1921.

title: Tocqueville's Democracy in America
body: After travelling through the United States in 1831–32, the French aristocrat Alexis de Tocqueville published Democracy in America in two volumes, in 1835 and 1840. He admired Americans' local self-government and voluntary associations, but warned of the 'tyranny of the majority' and of a soft despotism of conformity. It is a classic analysis of democratic society.

title: The Law of the Sea Convention
body: Concluded in 1982 after nearly a decade of negotiation, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sets the legal framework for the world's oceans. It fixes territorial waters at up to 12 nautical miles and gives coastal states exclusive economic zones of up to 200 nautical miles, while treating the deep seabed beyond national jurisdiction as the common heritage of mankind.

title: The Meiji Constitution
body: Promulgated in 1889, the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was the first modern constitution in East Asia. Modelled largely on Prussia's, it created an elected lower house in a parliament called the Diet but kept sovereignty with the emperor and gave the armed forces direct access to him. That weak civilian control is often seen as helping militarists dominate government in the 1930s.
